newsitem.title: UK: Zinc firm as LME mulls fate of Asturiana position.
newsitem.headline: Zinc firm as LME mulls fate of Asturiana position.

text.p: Zinc prices rose strongly during the last week on what traders say are rumours that a big loss-making long position originally held by Spanish producer Asturiana de Zinc had been liquidated or transferred.

Last December the position was passed to Swiss-based trader Glencore International AG to manage, but traders and analysts now understand Glencore may have ended its involvement either by liquidating the position or passing it on.
The futures position on the London Metal Exchange (LME) had been blamed for zinc's poor performance over the last two years.

The rumours, as yet unconfirmed, of its liquidation or transfer to someone who was willing to hang on to it and play it was therefore seen as a bullish development, traders said, citing them as a market factor. Further fuelling the excitement was talk that financier George Soros had upped his stake in zinc, possibly by taking on some or all of the Asturiana position.

"Zinc prices leapt out from their range at the beginning of this week, and the (Soros) rumour has been a factor," said Adam Rowley, analyst at Macquarie Equities. "It is making people feel a bit more bullish about the market."
On Monday benchmark three month LME zinc futures rose to a three-month high of $1,055 a tonne against $1,039 at the close the previous Friday. The market traded down to $1,018 last week.
Rumours about the Asturiana position and Soros' possible involvement in zinc started the move, triggering chart-based buying from London-based funds, LME traders said.
The market has since retraced to around $1,045, partly because of weakness in the copper market and partly because of heavy Chinese selling, they added.

The position was loss-making because Asturiana started to accumulate it in 1992 when prices averaged over $1,200. But in 1993, when the position reached a peak, the average was $978.50. Analysts said it grew to over one million tonnes during 1993.
Asturiana said the position was reduced by half by March 1996, although it was "still substantial."
"We have heard strong rumours that Glencore has disposed of the position," said a base metals analyst.
"It is just a question of whether is gone completely or passed into someone else's hands," an equity analyst added.
If the position has gone completely it removes a significant cap from the zinc market, traders said.
If the position has passed into the hands of a fund player like Soros, the implications are also seen as bullish.
"If a speculator like Soros has the position, then he will be far more interested in holding on to it and seeing the price run higher," said one dealer.

Equity experts said they had also heard Soros had moved into zinc, but some were doubtful he would do so in the form of taking on the Asturiana position or buying Asturiana shares, as has also been rumoured.
On Tuesday last week Asturiana shares rose to 1,015 Spanish pesetas against a low of 858 pesetas the week before.
"On balance funds generally would seek to play the metal market rather than through direct involvement with a smelter," one said.
This would fit in with talk of funds buying LME zinc futures and options, the equity analyst said.
Traders and analysts said the zinc price may be capped by Chinese selling and still plentiful LME stocks over the next few months. But the outlook for 1997 was positive.
"Next year we are forecasting an average cash price of 54.5 cents per pound ($1,202/tonne)," Macquarie's Rowley said.
